data.name: AboutTitle
data.value: Os Diaples d'a Uerba

data.name: AboutHeroHeading
data.value: Who are the Diaples?

data.name: AboutHeroLead
data.value: Os Diaples d'a Uerba are a cultural association from Zaragoza. Our volunteer-based group creates theatrical shows full of music, fire and pyrotechnics, rescuing Aragonese traditions and mythological beings such as diaples, diaplerons, bruxas, bruxos, giants, lacuercos and other creatures.

data.name: AboutQuote
data.value: “We play with evil to do good—and make it more fun.”

data.name: AboutVolunteerParagraph
data.value: Our volunteers span all ages; we’re driven by the joy of performing and by working together to bring the group, its shows and performances wherever we are invited. Our goal is to enjoy ourselves and help others enjoy the party.

data.name: AboutIdentityParagraph
data.value: We are Diaples: those who were, those who are and those who will be.

data.name: AboutWhatAreDiaplesHeading
data.value: What are the diaples?

data.name: AboutWhatAreDiaplesParagraph1
data.value: They are mythological figures from Aragonese tradition, especially from the Pyrenees. They represent small restless beings—tiny little devils or goblins—who never stop misbehaving. The diapleron is the elder figure who carries the diaples in a hollow branch (cañoto) and can hand it over to a villager as a personal challenge.

data.name: AboutWhatAreDiaplesParagraph2
data.value: The diaples that live inside the cañoto can be released to complete any tasks they are given. But if left idle, their restlessness may harm the owner of the cañoto and they can be freed to cause all sorts of havoc and mischief.

data.name: AboutOtherBeingsHeading
data.value: Other mythological beings

data.name: AboutMythDiaplerons
data.value: Diaplerons

data.name: AboutMythDiapleronsDescription
data.value: The elder who guides the diaples. They carry the cañoto where the little devils travel and can entrust it to someone willing to take on the challenge of controlling them.

data.name: AboutMythBruxas
data.value: Bruxas and bruxons

data.name: AboutMythBruxasDescription
data.value: Witches and warlocks of the Pyrenees; herbs, prayers and potions. They lead covens and are said to cast the evil eye, yet they also heal and chase away storms.

data.name: AboutMythEncantarias
data.value: Encantarias

data.name: AboutMythEncantariasDescription
data.value: Enchanted women who appear near springs, rivers or caves—especially on Saint John's Eve—to guard treasures or ask favours in exchange for secrecy.

data.name: AboutMythFadas
data.value: Fadas

data.name: AboutMythFadasDescription
data.value: Aragonese fairies, usually benevolent yet capricious: they help those who respect the forest and their word, and punish those who break promises.

data.name: AboutMythChigans
data.value: Chigans

data.name: AboutMythChigansDescription
data.value: Playful travelling sprites: they move things around, play tricks and vanish without a trace. Sometimes they protect children when treated kindly.

data.name: AboutMythOmes
data.value: Omes Granizos

data.name: AboutMythOmesDescription
data.value: “Hail men”: storm spirits who herd the clouds. Village spells tried to divert them to save the crops.

data.name: AboutMythLacuerco
data.value: Lacuerco

data.name: AboutMythLacuercoDescription
data.value: A hairy serpent that, according to tradition, slipped into cradles to nurse from the mother while soothing the baby with its tail. People sprinkled ash around the crib to detect its trail the next morning.

data.name: AboutHistoryHeading
data.value: History of the group

data.name: AboutHistoryParagraph1
data.value: Diaples d’a Uerba was born in a curious way. It began with the idea of livening up a carnival in Zaragoza, with diaples throwing fireworks along the parade. The following year a group gathered for the San Chuan de Plan carnival to protest the Aragón–Cazaril power line. They adopted the outfit that would later define the group, around 1991.

data.name: AboutHistoryParagraph2
data.value: The troupe belonged to the Ligallo de Fablans de l’Aragonés and saw the Diaples as a way to support the association, becoming the colla Diaples d’a Uerba. Their purpose was to spread Aragonese customs and traditions—language, dances, music, stick dances—defending a culture of fire with a manifesto against injustice: “Cremando inchusticias”.

data.name: AboutHistoryParagraph3
data.value: In early 2003 they separated from the association due to differing opinions and, in March, became the non-profit association Os Diaples d’a Uerba. Independence allowed them to decide freely with every member having a voice. We work as volunteers—with commitment, assembly-based decision-making and a horizontal structure.

data.name: AboutHistoryParagraph4
data.value: We keep the same goals as in the beginning: looking forward, creating new perspectives, studying, researching and helping anyone who asks. We want everyone to enjoy our shows as much as we do. Our ambition is a better world; until it arrives, we create celebrations to make ourselves known and welcome every gesture, even a smile.

data.name: AboutHistoryParagraph5
data.value: The group has changed and evolved over time. Some people leave, others join and new ones take part. We are a living entity that survives and adapts to its surroundings, always ensuring celebration and fun. Diaples: one big family.
